name: Japanese bush warbler
lede: Japanese bush warbler is a muted olive-brown named for a small songbird, and one of the most common named colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: In Japan: Uguisu-iro
sections.body:
The name is written 鶯色, romanized Uguisu-iro, literally "bush-warbler-colored," after the small Japanese bush warbler (*uguisu*), whose song is a familiar sound of early spring in Japan [1]. A darker, browner variant of the same name, [[japanese-bush-warbler-brown]], is listed alongside it as a family member [1]. Our library gives no date for when the name was first fixed to this shade [1].

The nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[acanthe]], almost the same shade; [[brownish-olive]] sits close by, duller [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a match for Japanese bush warbler in 4,878 of 23,781 paintings, about 20.5 percent, more common than 98 percent of the named colors we track, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 500 of 3,449 paintings from that century, 1.2 times the rate its share of the archive would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 37 percent of its appearances [3].

The painter most devoted to it is Jean-Charles Cazin, in 8 of his 16 paintings here, 2.7 times his peers' rate, as photographed [3]. The earliest archive match is dated 1000; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with the colors we call Gold Fusion and Water Grey [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications [3].
